note: Correct as stated for this context; an opinion about the importance of relational databases, which remain the most widely deployed database model (Codd's model became the standard for financial, personnel and logistics records per IBM's history).

Rows and columns is right, but the name does not come from relationships between tables. In Codd's model a 'relation' is the table itself: a set of tuples, with 'relation' used in its mathematical sense. Foreign-key relationships are useful but they are not where the name 'relational' comes from. Picking a relational database 'for relations' between entities is a fine rule of thumb; calling that the reason for the name is a common interview mistake.
precise_version: A relational database stores data as relations (tables of rows and columns); the name comes from the mathematical 'relation' (a set of tuples), and links between tables are expressed with keys.

note: Correct as stated for this context (opinion on the historical role of relational databases; IBM's history page describes them as the standard for financial records, bank accounts, credit-card data and ATM transactions).
A generalisation offered as the teacher's view ('always' finds first use in finance). Not a checkable technical claim; harmless framing.

Personal anecdote about the teacher's father's machine and tools; no public source can confirm it. That accounting/ledger work was an early business use of computers is uncontroversial and not misleading.

Blockchain was not introduced around 2012. Satoshi Nakamoto announced the Bitcoin paper ('Bitcoin P2P e-cash paper') on the cryptography mailing list on 31 October 2008, and the network started in January 2009. The teacher's point (first applications were about money) still stands: Bitcoin was an electronic cash system.
precise_version: Blockchain arrived with Bitcoin (paper published October 2008, network live January 2009), and its first application was money.

note: Codd's 1970 paper, 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks', was a general model for storing and accessing information in large shared databases without knowing their physical layout. It was not designed specifically for accounting. The rows-and-columns form comes from the mathematical relation (a set of tuples), not from copying ledgers. Finance became one of the main users later: IBM calls relational databases the standard for financial records, bank accounts and ATM transactions.
precise_version: Relational databases were designed as a general model for large shared data banks; finance became one of their biggest early users, and the table shape comes from the mathematical 'relation', not from accounting ledgers.

note: Correct as stated for this context; PostgreSQL docs: indexes speed up retrieval 'But indexes also add overhead to the database system as a whole, so they should be used sensibly' (every insert/update/delete must also maintain each index).

Strong guarantees mattered because money was involved, but ACID was not part of the original relational model. Codd's 1970 model is about data structure and querying. The transaction properties were formalised separately: Jim Gray described atomicity, consistency and durability in 1981, and the acronym ACID comes from Haerder and Reuter's 1983 paper. Relational systems such as System R and its successors implemented these transactions. Finance was one big driver of that, not the only one.
Correct as stated for this context; durability is 'the survival of a committed transaction's effects after failures' and atomicity is all-or-nothing, which is what financial use needs.
Correct as stated for this context; deadlock detection/prevention is a general concurrency topic that applies to OS threads, database locks and distributed transactions alike.
Correct as stated for this context (learning advice).
The teacher's own experience (85% built himself); no public source can confirm it.
Correct as stated for this context (opinion on teaching value of the demo).

Right answer. One point a reader needs: the 'I' in ACID only goes as far as the isolation level allows. Defaults are weaker than serializable (InnoDB uses REPEATABLE READ, PostgreSQL uses READ COMMITTED), so a read-then-write pattern like 'read the free seat, then book it' can race unless you use explicit locking reads or a conditional UPDATE. ACID being 'on' does not by itself rule out such races.

At commit, InnoDB does not flush the changed data pages. It flushes the redo log (write-ahead log) and writes the pages later. Durability also depends on configuration: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 (the default, MySQL 8.4) writes and flushes the log at each commit. With 0 or 2 the log is flushed about once per second, and transactions whose log was not flushed 'can be lost in a crash'.
precise_version: Durability: when you commit, the transaction's log record is flushed to disk (with the default settings), so the change survives a crash.

note: Correct as stated for this context; InnoDB offers the four SQL:1992 levels READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.

SERIALIZABLE does not mean the database runs one transaction at a time. It guarantees the result is the same as some serial order, while transactions still run concurrently. PostgreSQL 18 uses Serializable Snapshot Isolation: it adds no blocking beyond Repeatable Read and instead aborts conflicting transactions with a serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001) that the application must retry. InnoDB's SERIALIZABLE is REPEATABLE READ with plain SELECTs turned into SELECT ... FOR SHARE (when autocommit is off), so it blocks on locks and can deadlock. So it is slower, but not because of literal serial execution. And the seat-booking problem turns into retries or deadlocks, not into 'no problem at all'.
precise_version: SERIALIZABLE guarantees the outcome equals some one-at-a-time order; databases enforce it with extra locking (MySQL) or by aborting conflicting transactions for retry (PostgreSQL), which costs throughput.

note: Correct as stated for this context; defaults are not serializable: InnoDB default is REPEATABLE READ (MySQL 8.4), PostgreSQL default is READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL 18).

Isolation is configurable and the default is not serializable, so that part is right. 'With serializable you would not need all this locking' needs a caveat: under PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE the application must catch serialization failures and retry, and under InnoDB SERIALIZABLE the implicit shared locks on reads can make two bookers deadlock. You trade explicit locks for retry handling.

The main point (relational databases handle high QPS well with good queries) is fair. 'They cannot handle big data' is an over-generalisation: sharded relational setups run at very large scale. Vitess, a clustering system for horizontal scaling of MySQL, 'served all YouTube database traffic for over five years'. The fair version: a single relational node is not built for analytics-scale data, and scaling it takes partitioning or sharding.
Correct as stated for this context; MySQL server is written in C and C++, and its concurrency code uses signal/wait (condition-variable/event) terminology.

A plain UPDATE does lock: in InnoDB, 'UPDATE ... WHERE ...' sets exclusive locks on the records it scans, and a second UPDATE of the same row blocks until the first commits or rolls back. That happens at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ alike, so the queuing comes from row locks, not from the isolation level. The isolation level decides what happens after the wait. PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED re-checks the WHERE clause against the new row version and applies the update. PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ/SERIALIZABLE abort with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update'. InnoDB re-reads the latest committed row. The student's guess ('cancelled') is right for PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ.
precise_version: A plain UPDATE takes an exclusive row lock, so concurrent updates of the same row queue; the isolation level decides whether the waiter then re-checks and proceeds (read committed) or is aborted for retry (PostgreSQL repeatable read / serializable).

note: The syntax half is right: FOR UPDATE is a clause of SELECT, not of UPDATE. 'You have never acquired a lock on any row' is wrong. MySQL 8.4: 'UPDATE ... WHERE ... sets an exclusive next-key lock on every record the search encounters' (only a record lock when matching a unique row via a unique index). A locking read is defined as locking rows 'the same as if you issued an UPDATE statement for those rows'. UPDATE does not need FOR UPDATE because it always takes the exclusive lock itself.
precise_version: You cannot write FOR UPDATE on an UPDATE, and you don't need to: an UPDATE always takes an exclusive lock on the rows it touches, which is exactly the lock SELECT ... FOR UPDATE takes.

LIMIT is not just a final filter after all data has been read. Optimizers use it to read less. MySQL 8.4: 'As soon as MySQL has sent the required number of rows to the client, it aborts the query', and with ORDER BY on an index it stops early. PostgreSQL: 'The query optimizer takes LIMIT into account when generating query plans'. The teacher's point holds for OFFSET and for queries that must sort or aggregate everything first (filesort, GROUP BY): 'The rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient.'
precise_version: LIMIT lets the database stop early when rows come out in the right order (for example via an index), but rows skipped by OFFSET, and everything before a full sort or aggregation, are still read and computed.

note: Correct as stated for this context; ORMs can generate inefficient query patterns, e.g. the per-object 'deluge of database queries' when accessing related objects that Django's select_related/prefetch_related exist to stop.

The trade-off (speed of development vs control) is fair, but mainstream ORMs do provide escape hatches for stored procedures. Django's cursor has callproc(), which 'Calls a database stored procedure with the given name', and Manager.raw() runs raw SQL that returns model instances. The support is plain rather than missing.
Engineering opinion (ORMs fine at mid-scale, worst at high scale); reasonable but not a checkable fact.
Correct as stated for this context (pragmatic advice: ORM for early shipping velocity).

True by default, since an ORM model query loads all fields. ORMs do offer projections, though: Django's only()/defer() load just the named fields and values() returns dicts. Whether that hurts readability is opinion. A careful reader should know that the projection exists and is one call away.

Opinion on readability. For context: Django's prefetch_related retrieves related objects 'in a single batch' and, with select_related, is 'designed to stop the deluge of database queries' caused by lazy relation access, so it is an optimisation tool, whatever one thinks of its ergonomics.
Correct as stated for this context; Django documents two raw paths: Manager.raw() and executing custom SQL directly via a cursor.

Too general. Pooling is usually done by the driver or pool layer, and some ORMs are good at it: SQLAlchemy's engine 'has a QueuePool integrated, pre-configured with reasonable pooling defaults' (pool size 5). The complaint fits Django well, though: CONN_MAX_AGE defaults to 0, which closes the database connection at the end of each request, and native psycopg pooling only arrived in Django 5.1.
Correct as stated for this context; mixing ORM with raw SQL for complex queries is a supported, documented pattern (Django Manager.raw / cursor).
Opinion on readability of complex joins in ORM vs SQL; not a checkable fact.

In spirit this is how major engines work inside, but the main reason is MVCC, not B+ tree rebalancing. InnoDB 'does not physically remove a row from the database immediately when you delete it'; the row is delete-marked and later removed by purge once no transaction needs it for MVCC or rollback. PostgreSQL likewise keeps the old row version until VACUUM reclaims it, because 'the row version must not be deleted while it is still potentially visible to other transactions'. This internal delete-marking is invisible to queries, which is different from an application-level soft-delete column.
Correct as stated for this context (teaching choice / learning advice).
The teacher's own war story (deadlocks then throughput problems); not publicly verifiable, and plausible.

Fair as a design philosophy. Note that standard SQL does have a built-in feature close to this: SQL:2011 system-versioned temporal tables (SQL Server 2016+, MariaDB). On DELETE, 'The system stores the previous value of the row in the history table' and removes it from the current table, giving deleted-row recovery and auditing without a hand-made is_deleted column. Many relational engines therefore do offer something soft-delete-like, as an opt-in feature.
Correct as stated for this context (reasoning about developer cognitive load of built-in soft deletes).

DynamoDB does not give users soft deletion. DeleteItem 'Deletes a single item in a table by primary key', and the item is gone from reads; there is no undelete flag (recovery means point-in-time restore or backups). AWS does not publicly document how storage reclaims space. The background, deferred deletion users can see is TTL: expired items are deleted 'within a few days of their expiration time, without consuming write throughput' and can appear in reads until then. So 'it always soft-deletes, so KV stores provide soft deletion' is not something a reader can rely on.
precise_version: DynamoDB has no user-facing soft delete: DeleteItem removes the item; its TTL feature deletes expired items lazily in the background (within days), so expired items must be filtered out of reads.
